definition: Storm damage roof repair restores the roof covering where a storm opened a detail — wind-lifted shingles, hail-bruised surfaces, debris punctures, or displaced flashing — and documents the damage for an insurance claim. It separates storm-caused damage from pre-existing wear, the distinction that governs coverage.

costRanges.source: HomeAdvisor and Angi cost data (per gold pricing.range / faq / pricing.factors)

costRanges.item: Hail-damage repair (by hail size and affected roof area)
costRanges.source: Angi storm-damage cost data (per gold pricing.factors / faq)

costRanges.range: NJ ranges sit 10–40% above national figures, because labor accounts for roughly 60% of a repair total and NJ code is stricter

Storm-damage roof repair is priced per repair / per affected component, not as one whole-roof total. Widespread damage above 25–30% of the roof area shifts the scope to full replacement under the contractor-consensus 25% rule. Newark Quality Roofing provides a free written estimate.

signs: Missing or wind-lifted shingles after high winds expose the underlayment and roof deck, and uplift concentrates at roof edges, rakes, and corners where wind damage starts — per IBHS wind research.

Circular bruises and granule loss on the shingle surface indicate hail impact, because hail damage begins at roughly 1.0 inch on aged 3-tab shingles and 1.25 inches on most asphalt products — per an American Meteorological Society hail-threshold study.
Dents on metal gutters, downspouts, and vent caps mark hail strikes, with the field benchmark being roughly 8 functional impacts per 100 square feet — per IBHS insurer-protocol guidance.
New ceiling or wall stains appearing after a storm that spread or darken after rainfall indicate an active leak through a storm-opened detail — per GAF and This Old House inspection guidance.

Rusted, lifted, or bent flashing displaced from chimneys, walls, skylights, and valleys ranks as the most common leak source, because flashing seals the transitions that roughly 90–95% of leaks trace back to — an industry estimate attributed to the NRCA.

Granule accumulation at downspout discharge exceeding normal levels indicates a storm stripped the shingle UV layer, and granule loss exceeding 30% of the surface is the common rule-of-thumb for beyond repair — per GAF.
selectionCriteria: Active New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration — required of every NJ contractor doing home improvement work (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136). NJ issues NO roofing license; this is a registration, not a license. Verify the 13VH registration number, which must appear on contracts and advertisements (N.J.S.A. 56:8-144).

Commercial general liability insurance of at least $500,000 per occurrence, required of a registered NJ Home Improvement Contractor (N.J.S.A. 56:8-142) — verify it with a Certificate of Insurance obtained directly from the carrier.

A written contract for any home-improvement work over $500, required by the NJ Home Improvement Practices regulations (N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2), specifying scope, materials, total price, and start/completion dates.
A detailed, itemized written estimate setting the scope, labor, materials, and timeline — the same documentation a roofing contractor provides to the insurance adjuster.

Established local presence and verifiable local references — a physical location in or near Essex County and a track record in the New Jersey market, the opposite of out-of-state storm chasers who leave when warranty issues arise.

Thorough documented storm assessment — timestamped photographs, measurements, and a written scope that separates storm-caused damage from pre-existing wear, the distinction that governs insurance coverage per Insurance Information Institute claims guidance.

Honest insurance-claim conduct — a contractor provides documentation and meets the adjuster on-site, but does NOT ask you to sign an Assignment of Benefits transferring your claim rights, promise to waive your deductible (insurance fraud in NJ), or inflate the damage claim.

technicalFacts.fact: Wind and hail rank as the largest homeowners-insurance claim type at 40.7% of homeowners claims and roughly 2.8% of insured homes per year (1 in 36), with an average claim of $14,747.

Separating storm-caused damage from pre-existing wear governs insurance coverage; hail leaves random-pattern circular bruises with granule loss, wind damage concentrates at roof edges, rakes, and corners where uplift peaks, and debris impact leaves directional damage, while uniform deterioration reads as wear.
technicalFacts.source: Insurance Information Institute claims guidance; IBHS wind and hail research

technicalFacts.fact: The share of partially unsealed field shingles rises from under 1% on roofs 0–6 years old to over 79% on roofs 14–20 years old, which is why wind damage starts at edges, rakes, and corners where tabs lift first.

Functional hail damage begins at roughly 1.0 inch on aged 3-tab shingles and 1.25 inches on most asphalt products; the field benchmark for hail damage is roughly 8 functional impacts per 100 square feet.
technicalFacts.source: American Meteorological Society hail-threshold study; IBHS insurer-protocol guidance

technicalFacts.fact: Roughly 90–95% of roof leaks originate at flashing, the most common leak source, which is why storm-displaced flashing at chimneys, walls, skylights, and valleys is a priority repair.
technicalFacts.source: Industry estimate attributed to the NRCA

technicalFacts.fact: Localized storm damage of a few shingles or a single puncture takes a targeted repair; damage above 25–30% of the roof area takes full replacement under the contractor-consensus 25% rule, with a second 50% rule favoring replacement when one repair approaches 50% of replacement cost.

Repair or replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family home counts as ordinary maintenance and requires no construction permit, inspection, or notice to the construction official.
On a commercial building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period requires a permit.
Most New Jersey homeowner policies require prompt notice of damage, interpreted as within 30 days of discovery, with a separate two-year statutory window for hurricane and named-storm losses.
technicalFacts.source: NJ Department of Banking and Insurance

technicalFacts.fact: A FORTIFIED roof made homes over 70% less likely to file a claim and cut damage 22% when a claim occurred, across 40,000-plus analyzed properties; the 2025 FORTIFIED standard requires asphalt shingles rated Excellent or Good on IBHS impact ratings to withstand hail up to 2 inches.

New Jersey averages roughly 25–30 thunderstorms per year that produce summer hail, and sees at least one coastal storm annually, with some years reaching 5–10 storm events; nor'easters and coastal storms strike most often October through April.
On low-slope commercial roofs, EPDM fails most often at the seams and TPO at the welded seams; EPDM lasts 15–25 years, TPO 7–20 years, and modified bitumen 20 years.
Storm-weakened materials and wet surfaces are fall hazards, so a sound storm assessment proceeds from the ground and the attic, not the roof surface.
Roof line items now exceed a quarter of all residential claim value, and non-catastrophic wind and hail losses rose from 17% to 25% of residential claims since 2022.

sources: NJ Department of Banking and Insurance
IBHS (Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety)

articleAngles.signs: Definitively answer the storm-damage warning signs: missing/wind-lifted shingles at edges/rakes/corners (IBHS uplift pattern), circular bruises + granule loss from hail (AMS thresholds ~1.0 in aged 3-tab / 1.25 in asphalt), dents on metal gutters/downspouts/vent caps (~8 functional impacts per 100 sf, IBHS), post-storm ceiling/wall stains (GAF, This Old House), displaced flashing (NRCA ~90–95% of leaks), and excess granules at the downspout (>30% surface loss rule, GAF). Frame storm-vs-wear distinction (governs coverage, III). Assess from the ground/attic, not the roof (OSHA). Use registered NJ HIC, insured — never 'licensed.'
articleAngles.costGuide: Definitively answer that storm-damage repair has no single whole-job total — it is priced per repair/component. Cite ONLY sourced figures: most repairs roughly $400–$2,000 (HomeAdvisor, Angi); hail repair $3,000–$12,000 by hail size and roof area (Angi); flashing reseal/small section $200–$500 (Modernize); NJ runs 10–40% above national, labor ~60% of total (Integrity Home Exteriors). Damage >25–30% of roof area shifts to full replacement (contractor-consensus 25% rule). On insurance: thorough independent documentation — timestamped photos, measurements, written assessment — is what insurers weigh (III claims guidance); KILL the HAAG cite and all invented deductible/test-square figures. Free written estimate.
articleAngles.decision: Definitively answer how to choose a storm-damage roof repair contractor: verify active NJ HIC registration with the 13VH number on the contract/ad (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136 / 56:8-144 — registration, NOT a license), CGL insurance min $500,000/occurrence via a Certificate of Insurance from the carrier (N.J.S.A. 56:8-142), a written contract for work over $500 with a three-day cancellation right (N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2), a detailed itemized written estimate, verifiable local references and established local presence, and a thorough documented storm assessment. Flag improper conduct: no AOB that transfers claim rights, no deductible-waiver promise (NJ insurance fraud), no inflated damage. Reframe insurer disputes around documentation (III), not HAAG. Registered NJ HIC + insured, never 'licensed'; no 24/7 promise.
